question: What is microsatellite instability, how does loss of DNA mismatch repair produce it, and how does the origin of sporadic MSI colorectal cancer differ from Lynch syndrome-associated MSI?

key_points.point: When mismatch repair is lost, tumors become hypermutated, with errors concentrated in short repetitive (microsatellite) sequences; MSI is therefore used as a readout of dMMR.
Roughly 15% of colorectal cancers are MSI; about 3% of all colorectal cancers are Lynch-associated and about 12% are sporadic, so most MSI cases are not inherited.
In sporadic MSI-high colorectal cancer, MLH1 is silenced mainly by promoter hypermethylation (epigenetic) rather than by mutation.
MSI colorectal tumors are more often right-sided, rich in infiltrating lymphocytes and mucinous or poorly differentiated, and carry a modestly better prognosis than non-MSI tumors.

question: How do mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry, PCR-based microsatellite analysis, and next-generation sequencing compare as methods for determining MSI/dMMR status?

key_points.point: ESMO consensus recommends IHC for the four MMR proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) as the first test, with PCR of a five-marker panel including BAT-25 and BAT-26 as the second method.
MSI status can be inferred from large targeted NGS panels (MSIsensor score) with about 99% concordance with MSI-PCR and/or MMR IHC in colorectal and endometrial cancers.
NGS-based MSI calling finds MSI-high tumors in cancer types that are not routinely screened and can be combined with tumour mutational burden analysis when selecting patients for immunotherapy.
Among colorectal cancer patients meeting the revised Bethesda criteria, MSI testing and MMR immunostaining were equally effective at selecting patients for germline MSH2/MLH1 testing.

question: Does MSI-high/mismatch repair-deficient status predict response to PD-1 blockade, and what did randomized evidence show for first-line treatment of metastatic MSI-high colorectal cancer?

key_points.point: In the first phase 2 pembrolizumab study, mismatch repair-deficient colorectal cancers responded (40% immune-related response) while proficient ones did not (0%), and deficient tumors carried far more somatic mutations.
An expanded cohort spanning 12 tumor types showed objective responses in about half of dMMR patients (21% complete), supporting a tissue-agnostic effect attributed to high neoantigen load.

In the phase 3 KEYNOTE-177 trial, first-line pembrolizumab roughly doubled median progression-free survival versus chemotherapy (16.5 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.60) in MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer.
Pembrolizumab caused fewer grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events than chemotherapy (22% vs 66%); overall survival was still immature at that analysis.

question: Do patients with MSI-high/dMMR stage II-III colon cancer benefit from adjuvant fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy?

key_points.point: In tumor specimens from randomized trials, fluorouracil-based adjuvant therapy improved survival for MSS/MSI-low tumors but showed no benefit for MSI-high tumors.
A validation study found no disease-free survival gain from fluorouracil-based adjuvant therapy in dMMR tumors, and in stage II dMMR disease treatment was associated with worse overall survival.
MSI-high status is prognostically favorable: untreated patients with MSI-high tumors had better overall survival than those with MSS/MSI-low tumors.

Evidence for oxaliplatin is weaker and observational: a retrospective multicenter cohort linked fluoropyrimidine plus oxaliplatin, but not fluoropyrimidine alone, to better disease-free survival, significant only in stage III dMMR disease.

question: Can PD-1 blockade alone replace chemoradiotherapy and surgery for mismatch repair-deficient locally advanced rectal cancer?

key_points.point: In a phase 2 trial of dostarlimab, all 12 patients who completed treatment achieved clinical complete response, and none had needed chemoradiotherapy or surgery at the time of the report.
A separate phase 2 study of neoadjuvant sintilimab reported a complete response (pathological or clinical) in 12 of 16 evaluable patients, with one case of primary resistance.
The evidence comes only from small single-arm studies with short follow-up, and both groups state that longer follow-up is needed to judge how durable the responses are.

question: How does digital PCR achieve absolute quantification of nucleic acids, and how does its principle differ from analog real-time PCR?

key_points.point: Digital PCR isolates single template molecules (by dilution or partitioning), amplifies them separately and reads each product individually, turning PCR's exponential analog signal into a linear digital count.
Each partition receives a discrete number of target molecules, and Poisson statistics of this partitioning underlie absolute quantification and its error sources.

Droplet digital PCR scales partitioning to very large numbers of reactions with standard TaqMan assays, enabling absolute copy-number measurement and detection of rare mutant DNA in a large wild-type excess.

question: Is droplet digital PCR more sensitive and more precise than quantitative real-time PCR?

key_points.point: In a head-to-head microRNA comparison, ddPCR gave better precision and day-to-day reproducibility than real-time PCR, but its sensitivity was comparable rather than superior.
ddPCR's advantage is clearest for low-abundance targets (Cq of 29 or more) and samples with variable inhibitory contaminants, where it gives more precise and reproducible results.
qPCR keeps advantages in dynamic range, sample volume and throughput, so the two methods are complementary rather than one being uniformly better.

question: How accurate is plasma droplet digital PCR for detecting EGFR and KRAS mutations in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer compared with tissue genotyping?

key_points.point: In a prospective validation, plasma ddPCR had 100% positive predictive value for EGFR exon 19 deletion, L858R and KRAS, while sensitivity was moderate (about 64-82% depending on the mutation).
Plasma ddPCR results were available in a median of 3 days, much faster than tissue genotyping.
Plasma T790M calls agreed less well with tissue (lower PPV/specificity), plausibly because of tumor heterogeneity, and digital platforms detected T790M better than non-digital ones.
Serial plasma ddPCR tracked response to erlotinib and picked up emerging T790M resistance as much as 16 weeks ahead of progression on imaging.

question: Can digital PCR be used for noninvasive prenatal detection of fetal trisomies, and how strong is the evidence for its diagnostic accuracy?

key_points.point: Digital PCR detects trisomy 21 by counting molecules to show over-representation of chromosome 21 relative to a reference chromosome, an approach that works without relying on allelic (SNP) differences.
Early proof-of-concept work detected trisomy 21 at a fetal DNA fraction of 25%.
A 2024 meta-analysis of six studies estimated pooled sensitivity of about 98% and specificity of about 99% for trisomy 21 against karyotyping.
Data for trisomies 18 and 13 were too sparse for meta-analysis, and clinical applicability and advantages over NGS-based screening remain to be established.

question: What experimental design and reporting practices are recommended to make digital PCR results reliable, and what are the main sources of measurement error?

key_points.point: The dMIQE guidelines set out minimum information to report for digital PCR experiments, so that results can be independently evaluated.
Even though dPCR may offer better reproducibility and tolerance of inhibitors than qPCR, reliable results still depend on careful assay design and proper controls.

The 2020 update flags threshold setting during data analysis and pre-analytical steps (purifying, concentrating or modifying nucleic acids) as sources of measurement error, and simplifies the reporting table.
The partitioning statistics themselves (Poisson) introduce error sources that must be accounted for in quantification.

question: What is circulating tumor DNA, how does it relate to the total cell-free DNA in plasma, and how does its detectability vary across cancer types and stages?

key_points.point: ctDNA is the tumor-derived fraction of plasma cell-free DNA carrying somatic mutations; mutant fragments are greatly outnumbered by normal cfDNA, so highly sensitive assays are needed.
ctDNA was detectable in over 75% of patients with many advanced cancers but in under half with primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers, and less often in localized than advanced disease.
Tumor-derived cfDNA is enriched in shorter fragments (about 90-150 bp), and selecting this size range improves ctDNA detection.
Serial ctDNA measurements track tumor dynamics during surgery and chemotherapy.

question: Can postoperative ctDNA testing be used to guide adjuvant chemotherapy decisions in stage II colon cancer?

key_points.point: In resected stage II colon cancer without adjuvant therapy, detectable postoperative ctDNA was strongly associated with recurrence (HR about 18), whereas most ctDNA-negative patients did not recur.
In the randomized DYNAMIC trial, ctDNA-guided management cut adjuvant chemotherapy use (15% vs 28%) with noninferior 2-year recurrence-free survival.
With about 5 years of follow-up, recurrence-free and overall survival remained similar between ctDNA-guided and standard management.
Among treated ctDNA-positive patients, ctDNA clearance at the end of chemotherapy was associated with a far better recurrence-free outcome than persistent ctDNA.

question: How well does ctDNA-based detection of minimal residual disease after curative-intent treatment predict relapse, and how much lead time does it give over standard follow-up?

key_points.point: In stage I-III colorectal cancer, ctDNA positivity after surgery or after adjuvant chemotherapy was independently and strongly associated with relapse; every patient still ctDNA-positive after adjuvant chemotherapy relapsed.
Serial ctDNA monitoring in colorectal cancer flagged recurrence a mean of about 9 months before imaging, though it did not catch every relapse (14 of 16).
In early breast cancer, ctDNA after apparently curative treatment predicted metastatic relapse, and serial tracking gave a median lead time of about 8 months over clinical relapse.
In early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer, tumor-informed phylogenetic ctDNA profiling of postoperative plasma identified patients very likely to relapse and tracked the subclonal makeup of relapse.

question: How well do cell-free DNA-based multi-cancer early detection blood tests detect early-stage cancer, and has a screening benefit been established?

key_points.point: In the CCGA validation set, a methylation-based MCED test had about 99.5% specificity but overall sensitivity near 51%, ranging from about 17% in stage I to about 90% in stage IV.

CancerSEEK, which combines cfDNA mutations with protein markers, had over 99% specificity in healthy controls and a median sensitivity of about 70% across eight types of already-diagnosed, nonmetastatic cancers.
In the prospective PATHFINDER screening cohort, a cancer signal appeared in 1.4% of participants, and most positives (62%) turned out to be false positives.
PATHFINDER only supports feasibility; its authors call for further research on clinical utility, so these studies do not show a benefit on cancer outcomes.

question: Why can somatic mutations detected in plasma cell-free DNA fail to reflect the tumor genotype, and how can such false positives be reduced?

key_points.point: Most cfDNA comes from blood cells, so non-malignant mutations from clonal hematopoiesis can appear in plasma and be mistaken for tumor variants.
In high-depth cfDNA sequencing, most mutations found in non-cancer controls (about 82%) and about half of those in cancer patients had features of clonal hematopoiesis.
Genes commonly mutated in clonal hematopoiesis are most affected: in lung cancer patients, most plasma JAK2 mutations, some TP53 and rare KRAS mutations came from blood cells rather than the tumor.
Sequencing matched white blood cell DNA alongside cfDNA is recommended so that blood-derived variants are not misattributed to the tumor.
